passage: Manoj's tower of steel tumblers crashed across the kitchen floor of the Pune flat, and Pradeep shouted, "Enough! Pick them up now!" Manoj froze, then howled. Pradeep breathed out slowly and knelt beside him. "That was too loud. I'm sorry I shouted. You got a big fright, didn't you?" Manoj sniffed and nodded against his father's shoulder. "You wanted the tower to reach the shelf." "It fell," Manoj whispered. Pradeep rubbed his back until the sobs slowed. Then they gathered the tumblers together, one clink at a time.

qa.q: What did Manoj build that crashed onto the floor?
qa.a: He built a tower of steel tumblers, and it crashed across the kitchen floor.

qa.q: How was Manoj feeling right after his father shouted, and what shows it?
qa.a: He was frightened and upset; he froze and then howled.

qa.q: What turning point came after Pradeep shouted, and why did it help?
qa.a: Pradeep breathed out, knelt down and said sorry for being too loud, which turned a scolding into comfort so Manoj could settle.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel after shouting at Manoj?
qa.a: Pradeep may feel sorry and a little ashamed of being so loud, which is why he breathes out, kneels and apologises.

grounding: A father repairs after shouting, puts his son's fright into words and stays calmly beside him until the child settles.

passage:
"Mumma, you said you'd come before the story!" Sumit's face is wet.
"I did say that. And I came late. I'm sorry, Sumit."
"You always come late!" He kicks the blanket off.
"You're angry. Maybe a bit sad too?"
"Sad. I waited and waited."
"Waiting that long is hard. Can I sit here?"
He shrugs. Leela sits on the edge of the bed and says nothing for a while.
"Will you read now?"
"One story now. And tomorrow I'll set an alarm so I leave the office on time."
"Two stories."
"One story and a long cuddle."
Sumit scoots over to make room.

qa.q: What does Leela say she will do tomorrow?
qa.a: She says she will set an alarm so she leaves the office on time.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling while he waited, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt sad and let down; his face is wet, he kicks the blanket off and says he waited and waited.

qa.q: Which choice helped at the moment Sumit was angriest?
qa.a: Leela admitted she came late, said sorry and named his anger and sadness instead of arguing, so he calmed enough to let her sit with him.

qa.q: What would change if Leela had said, "Stop fussing, I'm here now"?
qa.a: Sumit would likely stay upset and feel his waiting didn't matter; the apology and the quiet sitting helped him trust her again.

grounding: A mother who came home late owns her mistake, names her son's feelings and sits calmly with him until he makes room for her.

passage: Pickup note, Thursday. Saurabh's painting tore as he ran out, and he flung himself on the mat, sobbing. His mother, Chandrika, snapped first: "Get up, we're late!" Then she stopped, knelt beside him and waited. "You're sad your rocket ripped. I shouted just now, and I'm sorry." He leaned into her. They taped the rocket together on the bench. I have seen her lose patience before, and I have seen her come back every time; he still runs to her. Next step: I gave them extra tape for home.

qa.q: What happened to Saurabh's painting?
qa.a: Saurabh's painting tore as he ran out.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling on the mat, and how did it change?
qa.a: He was upset and sad about his ripped rocket; once his mother knelt, named it and said sorry, he seemed comforted and leaned into her.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do after snapping that other parents could copy?
qa.a: She stopped, knelt, named Saurabh's sadness and apologised for shouting, which turned a slip into a repair.

qa.q: How does the note-writer see Chandrika as a parent?
qa.a: The note-writer sees that she is not perfect and loses patience, but she comes back every time, which is why Saurabh still runs to her.

grounding: Shows a parent who snaps, then repairs, names her child's sadness and stays calmly beside him.

passage: The anganwadi gate was already shut when Saurabh's father, Kamal, came running from the sugarcane field. Saurabh stood by the helper, face wet, fists tight. Kamal crouched in the dust. "You were frightened I wasn't coming. I was late, and that was my mistake." Saurabh hit his shoulder once, then climbed into his lap. Kamal didn't scold. He just held him till the hiccups slowed. On the walk home past the pond, Saurabh made him promise: "Tomorrow, early." Kamal tied a red thread on his own wrist to remember.

qa.q: Where was Kamal coming from when he reached the anganwadi?
qa.a: He came running from the sugarcane field.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh hit Kamal's shoulder and then climb into his lap?
qa.a: He was frightened and angry that his father was late, yet he still trusted him enough to seek comfort from him.

qa.q: What did Kamal do that helped Saurabh settle?
qa.a: He crouched down, named the fear, admitted the lateness was his mistake and held Saurabh without scolding until he calmed.

qa.q: What would change if Kamal had scolded Saurabh for crying?
qa.a: Saurabh might learn that his fear is not welcome and feel less safe turning to his father the next time he is scared.

grounding: Illustrates a parent staying calm, naming a child's fear and owning his own mistake of arriving late.

passage: Thunder cracked over the flats in Haifa, and Noa, five, shrieked from her bed. Her father, Yosef, half asleep, called out, "It's only noise, go to sleep!" The crying got louder. He sighed, padded in and sat on the floor beside her. "That was a big bang. You got scared, and I answered too fast. Sorry." Noa peeked out from the blanket. He counted with her between each flash and rumble, slowly. By the last flash she was counting on her own, one hand still holding his sleeve.

qa.q: Where did Yosef sit when he came into Noa's room?
qa.a: He sat on the floor beside her.

qa.q: How was Noa feeling by the end of the storm, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt calmer and safer; she was counting on her own while still holding his sleeve for comfort.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and how did Yosef fix it?
qa.a: He brushed off her fear from the other room; he then came in, named that she was scared, said sorry for answering too fast and counted with her.

qa.q: If you were Noa, what would you want from a parent during a storm?
qa.a: Someone who comes close, takes the fear seriously and helps you feel steady, even if they got it wrong at first.

grounding: Shows a father repairing a dismissive first reply by naming his child's fear and calmly staying with her.

passage:
In the clinic waiting room, Yash kicked the chair leg and wailed, "I want to go home!" Earlier, in the long queue, Payal had snapped, "Stop whining!" and his lip had trembled.
Now she knelt in front of him. "You're scared about the injection, and you're tired of waiting. That's a lot."
He nodded, sniffing.
"And Mumma was sharp with you in the queue. I'm sorry. I was tired too, but I shouldn't have shouted."
Yash climbed into her lap. When the nurse called his name, he held her finger tight and walked in.

qa.q: What had Payal snapped at Yash in the queue?
qa.a: She had snapped, "Stop whining!"

qa.q: What was Yash feeling in the waiting room?
qa.a: He was scared about the injection and tired of waiting; he kicked the chair and wailed that he wanted to go home.

qa.q: What did Payal do that helped Yash feel safe again?
qa.a: She knelt down calmly, named his fear and tiredness, and said sorry for shouting, which repaired the moment.

qa.q: What would change if Payal had never apologised for snapping?
qa.a: Yash might still feel hurt and unsure of her, and be less likely to lean on her when he walked in to the nurse.

grounding: Shows a mother responding to her child's distress with calm presence, naming the feeling and repairing after her own sharp words.
